mainTopic: Measuring the תחום שבת through cities: a measurer versus someone whose עירוב is inside a city, a city on a ravine's edge, and the towns of גדר and חמתן.
overview: The amud opens with an attempt to find a source in the משנה for רבי יהושע בן לוי's rule about a תחום that ends exactly at the far end of a city. רבי אידי reads the משנה differently, as speaking about a נותן who placed his עירוב inside the city. The גמרא answers that only the end-of-city case was new. רב נחמן then says both readings of the משנה are correct: one speaks about a נותן and the other about a מודד. Next, רב יוסף teaches that a city on the edge of a ravine measures its תחום from the edge only if it has a four-אמות barrier, because the edge is frightening to use. He tries to prove this from רבי's ruling about the towns of גדר and חמתן. רב דימי, רב ספרא and רב דימי בר חיננא each explain that ruling differently, so it is no longer proof for the barrier rule. Finally, a new משנה teaches that whoever places his עירוב inside a city may walk all of it plus 2000 אמות. רבי עקיבא disagrees, and the משנה discusses a cave with and without residents and a מודד whose measurement ends inside a cave.

steps.title: Finishing the quote of the משנה used as proof
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא completes the quotation from the משנה: residents of a small city may not walk through all of a large city.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the people of a small city may not walk through the entire large city.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a quote from the משנה that it brought to support רבי יהושע בן לוי. This line sets up the next step, where the גמרא explains why this quote proves his rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lets people of a big city walk through all of a small city, but not the reverse. That one-sided ruling is the key detail. The גמרא will now ask what causes the difference.

keyTerms.meaning: The residents of a small city

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not a new ruling of the גמרא. It is the second half of a משנה quote that began on the previous amud.

phrases.english: And the residents of a small city may not
phrases.notes: We're still reading the משנה being quoted here.

phrases.english: walk through the entire large city.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין אַנְשֵׁי עִיר קְטַנָּה מְהַלְּכִין אֶת כׇּל עִיר גְּדוֹלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the משנה quotation begun on the previous amud as a proof for רבי יהושע בן לוי.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יהושע בן לוי's rule: if the measurement ends at the end of the city, the city counts as four אמות; if it ends in the middle, he gets only up to the end of his measurement.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה: אנשי עיר גדולה מהלכין את כל עיר קטנה, ואין אנשי עיר קטנה מהלכין את כל עיר גדולה.

steps.title: Explaining why the משנה proves the rule
steps.stepSummary: The difference must be that the small-city people's 2,000 אמות run out in the middle of the big city, while the big-city people's 2,000 אמות run out at the end of the small city.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? Is it not because for these people their measurement ran out in the middle of the city, and for those people their measurement ran out at the end of the city?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains its proof. The only reason for the different treatment of the two groups must be where each group's 2,000 אמות end.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone coming from a small city into a big one runs out of אמות partway through the city, so he cannot walk all of it. Someone coming from a big city into a small one reaches its far end, so the whole city counts as four אמות. That is exactly רבי יהושע בן לוי's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it not because…? (introduces a forced explanation)

steps.whyThisMatters: If this reading holds, רבי יהושע בן לוי's rule has a direct source in the משנה. That would refute רבי אידי, who said it had none.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
Is it not because these ones,
phrases.notes: The residents of the small city

phrases.english: their measure ran out in the middle of the city,
and these ones, their measure ran out at the end of the city.
phrases.notes: The residents of the large city

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the inference from the משנה quoted in step 1.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יהושע בן לוי's rule distinguishing a measurement that ends at the end of the city from one that ends in its middle.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The one-sided ruling of the משנה about big-city and small-city residents.

steps.title: רבי אידי reads the משנה differently
steps.stepSummary: רבי אידי reads the משנה so that both groups may walk the whole city. He explains it as speaking about a נותן, someone who placed his עירוב in the other city, so it teaches nothing about a מודד.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי אידי teaches the text as 'the residents of… the residents of…', and he explains it as speaking about someone who placed his עירוב there. But about someone who is measuring, we did not learn anything.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אידי blocks the proof. He holds that the משנה treats both groups the same and is talking about someone who put his עירוב inside the city, not someone measuring 2,000 אמות from outside.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If someone places his עירוב inside a city, that whole city becomes his home base for שבת, so he may walk all of it no matter its size. On this reading the משנה has no 'may not', and the question of where the measurement ends never comes up. So the משנה is no source for רבי יהושע בן לוי.

keyTerms.meaning: He reads the text as 'residents… residents…' (both permitted)
He sets it (the משנה) in a specific case
One who placed his עירוב (inside the city)
One who measures 2,000 אמות from his place outside the city

steps.confusionAlert: רבי אידי is not inventing a new law. He is changing the wording of the משנה (no 'ואין') and its case (a נותן, not a מודד) so it no longer proves the rule.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Idi teaches 'the residents of… the residents of…',
phrases.notes: In his version, both lines say the residents are allowed.

phrases.english: and he establishes it as referring to one who placed his eiruv there.
But about one who measures, we did not learn.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of steps 1–2 by rereading the משנה.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from this משנה for רבי יהושע בן לוי.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumes the wording 'ואין' and a case of measuring. רבי אידי reads both clauses as permissive and sets the משנה in the case of a נותן, so a מודד is never discussed.

steps.title: Challenge: a משנה does discuss a מודד
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי אידי's claim that we never learned about a מודד. It cites a משנה about a measurer whose 2,000 אמות end even in the middle of a cave.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we did not? But we learned: 'And as for the measurer, about whom they said that we give him 2,000 אמות, this applies even if the end of his measurement ends inside a cave!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי אידי's statement 'מודד לא תנן'. It shows that a משנה clearly talks about a מודד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says a מודד gets exactly 2,000 אמות even when they end partway inside a cave. That means he may enter only the part of the cave inside his limit, even though a cave is one enclosed space. This is just like a measurement ending in the middle of a city, so the משנה does deal with a measurer and with partial areas.

keyTerms.meaning: And did we not? But we learned! (opens a challenge from a משנה)

phrases.english: And did we not? But didn't we learn:
And as for the one measuring, about whom they said
that we give him two thousand cubits,
that applies even if the end of his measure finishes inside a cave!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the last clause of רבי אידי's דחיה in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אידי's claim 'אבל מודד לא תנן', that the משנה never deals with a measurer.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A משנה explicitly discusses a מודד whose measurement ends partway inside a cave. That case parallels a measurement ending in the middle of a city, so the משנה does teach about a measurer.

steps.title: The end-of-city case still needed to be taught
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the challenge. We did learn about a measure ending in the middle of a city, but we never learned the case where it ends at the end of the city, so the teaching was still needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case of the end of the city was what he needed to teach, because we did not learn that in a משנה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 4. Yes, a משנה teaches about a measure ending in the middle of a city. But the case where the 2,000 אמות end exactly at the end of the city was never taught, so a new teaching was still needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge said a משנה already covers a מודד, so nothing new was needed. The answer splits the cases. A measure ending in the middle of a city is already known. A measure ending at the end of the city is a new case, where the whole city counts like four אמות and the rest of the measure continues past it. So the statement still teaches something new.

keyTerms.meaning: The end (far edge) of the city
It was necessary for him (to teach)
Because we did not learn it (in a משנה)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up 'middle of the city' and 'end of the city.' The challenge proved only the middle case is already known. The answer says the end case is the new information.

phrases.english: The end of the city was necessary for him,
phrases.notes: The case where the 2,000 אמות end exactly at the city's far edge.

phrases.english: since we did not learn it.
phrases.notes: No משנה covers this case, so the teaching adds something new.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 4
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the case: middle-of-city is known, end-of-city is new
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה about a measure ending in a cave already covers every מודד case, so the teaching adds nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the middle-of-city case was taught. The end-of-city case needed its own teaching.

steps.title: רב נחמן says both versions of the משנה are correct
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן says that whoever reads the משנה as 'people may walk' is not wrong, and whoever reads it as 'people may not walk' is also not wrong.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: Whoever reads 'the people of (the small city may walk the whole big city)' is not mistaken. And whoever reads 'the people of (the small city) may not' is also not mistaken.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן goes back to the two ways of reading the משנה and says both are acceptable. This sets up his explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the reading 'may not walk' (steps 1–2) was set against רבי אידי's reading 'may walk' (step 3). רב נחמן does not choose one. He says each reading can be correct, which means each must be talking about a different case.

keyTerms.meaning: Whoever reads / learns (the text this way)

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said:
One who reads 'the residents of' does not err,
phrases.notes: The version saying the small-city people may walk the whole big city.

phrases.english: and one who reads 'the residents of may not' does not err.
phrases.notes: The version saying they may not walk the whole big city.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: מַאן דְּתָנֵי ״אַנְשֵׁי״ לָא מִשְׁתַּבַּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new approach that settles the clash between the two readings
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both versions of the משנה, 'may walk' and 'may not walk', are correct.

steps.title: Each version speaks about a different case
steps.stepSummary: The 'may walk' reading is about a נותן, someone who placed his עירוב in the city. The 'may not walk' reading is about a מודד, someone measuring his 2,000 אמות from outside.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whoever reads 'the people of (may walk)' is not mistaken, because he explains the משנה as talking about someone who placed his עירוב. Whoever reads 'the people of (may not walk)' is not mistaken, because he explains it as talking about someone who measures.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן explains how both readings can be right. Each one is about a different kind of person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A נותן placed his עירוב inside the city, so the whole city counts as his place and he may walk all of it. A מודד comes from outside with only 2,000 אמות, which can run out partway through a big city. Once the cases are separated, the two readings no longer contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: Because he explains it as talking about (a specific case)
One who places his עירוב (inside the city)
One who measures his 2,000 אמות (from outside)

steps.whyThisMatters: This נותן versus מודד split is the key to the whole סוגיא. Where your שבת place is located decides how much of the city you may walk.

phrases.english: One who reads 'the residents of' does not err —
as he establishes it as referring to one who places his eiruv.
phrases.notes: The same approach as רבי אידי in step 3.

phrases.english: And one who reads 'the residents of may not' does not err —
as he establishes it as referring to one who measures.
phrases.notes: The same approach as the reading in steps 1–2.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains רב נחמן's statement in step 6
steps.terutzResolutionType: Setting each reading in a different case (אוקימתא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two readings contradict each other, so only one can be right.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'May walk' is about a נותן. 'May not walk' is about a מודד.

steps.title: Filling in the missing words of the משנה
steps.stepSummary: Following the 'may not walk' reading, the גמרא says the משנה leaves words out and spells out the full text. Big-city people may walk the whole small city, but small-city people may not walk the whole big city. That applies to a מודד. Someone who placed his עירוב in either city may walk all of it and 2,000 אמות beyond.
steps.simpleTranslation: Words are missing from the משנה, and this is what it means: The people of a big city may walk the whole small city, but the people of a small city may not walk the whole big city. When is this said? About someone who measures. But someone who was in the big city and placed his עירוב in the small city, or was in the small city and placed his עירוב in the big city, may walk all of it and 2,000 אמות beyond it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rebuilds the full text of the משנה so that the 'may not' reading includes the נותן case too. It does this by adding a clause the משנה leaves unstated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'may not walk' rule is limited to a מודד, whose 2,000 אמות can run out inside the big city. An added clause covers a נותן. Wherever he placed his עירוב, he walks that entire city and then 2,000 אמות past it. So one reconstructed משנה holds both rulings, matching רב נחמן's split.

keyTerms.meaning: The text is missing words (and we fill them in)
And this is what it teaches
In what case is this said?
His עירוב, the food placed to set his שבת place

steps.whatToRemember: A מודד may not walk all of a big city, because his 2,000 אמות may run out in the middle. A נותן walks the entire city where his עירוב is, plus 2,000 אמות beyond.
steps.confusionAlert: Two cities are named in each case. 'He was in the big city' (מִי שֶׁהָיָה בְּעִיר גְּדוֹלָה) tells you where he started. 'He placed his עירוב in the small city' tells you which city becomes his שבת base. The city with the עירוב is the one he may walk completely.

phrases.english: And it is incomplete, and this is what it teaches:
The residents of a large city may walk
through the entire small city,
but the residents of a small city may not walk
through the entire large city.
In what case is this said? With regard to one who measures.
phrases.notes: This is the limit the גמרא adds to the משנה.

phrases.english: But one who was in the large city
and placed his eiruv in the small city,
or was in the small city
and placed his eiruv in the large city —
he may walk through all of it
phrases.notes: The whole city where his עירוב is.

phrases.english: and beyond it two thousand cubits.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the full text of the משנה according to the 'may not walk' reading in step 7
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adding missing words to the text (חסורי מחסרא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The 'may not walk' reading leaves no room for a נותן case.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה limits the 'may not' rule to a מודד and adds a clause letting a נותן walk the whole city plus 2,000 אמות.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The 'may not' reading covers both cases: a מודד is limited by his 2,000 אמות, and a נותן walks the whole city with his עירוב plus 2,000 אמות.

steps.title: A city on the edge of a ravine
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף, quoting רמי בר אבא in the name of רב הונא, says a city on a ravine's edge measures its 2,000 אמות from the ravine's edge only if it has a barrier four high. Otherwise each person measures from his own front door.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said that רמי בר אבא said that רב הונא said: A city that sits on the edge of a ravine: if there is a barrier four high in front of it, we measure its limit from the edge of the ravine. If not, we measure only from the entrance of each person's house.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching about how to measure the תחום שבת of a city that sits right at the edge of a ravine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a barrier, the whole strip up to the ravine counts as part of the city, so the 2,000 אמות start at the ravine's edge. Without a barrier, the city is not treated as one unit for measuring. Then each person counts his 2,000 אמות from his own doorway, which gives him less room.

keyTerms.meaning: We measure for it (the city's 2,000 אמות)
From the entrance of his house

steps.confusionAlert: Here the word 'four' (אַרְבָּעָה) does not say whether it means four טפחים or four אמות. The very next step fixes this: רב יוסף had taught four אמות.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף אָמַר רָמֵי בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַב הוּנָא:
phrases.english: Rav Yosef said that Rami bar Abba said that Rav Huna said:
phrases.notes: A chain of three names passing down one teaching.

phrases.english: A city that sits on the edge of a ravine,
if there is in front of it a barrier four high —
we measure for it from the edge of the ravine.
phrases.notes: The barrier makes the ravine's edge the city's border.

phrases.english: And if not —

phrases.aramaic: אֵין מוֹדְדִין לָהּ אֶלָּא מִפֶּתַח בֵּיתוֹ.
phrases.english: we measure for it only from the entrance of his house.
phrases.notes: Each person counts from his own doorway.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף אָמַר רָמֵי בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic. It moves from measuring between two cities to a city on a ravine's edge.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A city on a ravine's edge measures its תחום from the ravine's edge only if a barrier four high stands there. Otherwise each person measures from his own door.

steps.title: Why does this barrier need to be four cubits high?
steps.stepSummary: אביי reminds רב יוסף that he had taught them four אמות. He then asks why this barrier must be so much taller than every other barrier, which needs only four טפחים.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: You told us about this a barrier of four אמות. What is different here from all the barriers in the world, which need only four?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי questions the rule. Why does a ravine barrier need four אמות when every other barrier in הלכה needs only four טפחים?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually a barrier of four טפחים (about a foot) is enough to count as a halachic wall. Four אמות is about six times taller. אביי wants to know what makes this barrier different.

keyTerms.meaning: Four cubits, much taller than four handbreadths
The barriers of the world, meaning ordinary barriers

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:

phrases.aramaic: דַּקָּה אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת אֲמַרְתְּ לַן עֲלַהּ.
phrases.english: You told us about it a barrier of four cubits.
phrases.notes: אביי reminds his teacher what he had taught them.

phrases.english: What is different from all the barriers of the world
which are four (handbreadths)?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Makes clear that the 'four' in step 9 means four אמות, then challenges why the measure is so large.
steps.kashyaTarget: The four-אמות height required in step 9
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every other barrier in הלכה needs only four טפחים, so requiring four אמות here looks inconsistent.

steps.title: A ravine's edge is frightening to use
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers that other barriers protect a place that is not scary to use. A ravine's edge is scary, so only a tall barrier makes it truly usable.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: There, using the place is not frightening. Here, using the place is frightening.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף explains why the ravine barrier must be taller than other barriers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In ordinary cases, four טפחים is enough because people use the area normally anyway. At a cliff edge, people are afraid to come close. So the strip only becomes usable city space when a barrier tall enough to make people feel safe stands there, and that means four אמות.

phrases.english: He said to him:
There, the use is not frightening.
Here, the use is frightening.
phrases.notes: Standing at a drop is scary without a real wall.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's question from step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (חילוק): the danger at a ravine changes what counts as usable space.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A barrier of four טפחים should be enough here, just as it is everywhere else.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because a ravine's edge is frightening, only a four-אמות barrier makes the strip usable as part of the city.
steps.whatToRemember: A ravine barrier needs four אמות, not four טפחים, because a cliff edge is only usable with a tall, safe wall.

steps.title: Proof from the towns of גדר and חמתן
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף brings a ברייתא. רבי allowed people from גדר to walk down to חמתן on שבת, but not people from חמתן to walk up to גדר. The reason must be that גדר built a barrier and חמתן did not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: From where do I say this? As it was taught in a ברייתא: רבי permitted the people of גדר to go down to חמתן, but the people of חמתן may not go up to גדר. What is the reason? Is it not because these built a barrier and those did not build a barrier?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף brings a source that supports his rule about a barrier at the edge of a slope.
steps.deeperAnalysis: גדר sat at the top of a slope and built a barrier at its edge. So its 2,000 אמות were counted from that edge and reached חמתן. חמתן had no barrier at its edge, so its people counted from their own houses and fell short of גדר. This explains why the permission worked in only one direction.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do I say this? (introducing a proof)
Two towns: גדר at the top of a slope, חמתן at the bottom
Is it not because...? (pointing to the obvious reason)

steps.whyThisMatters: The ברייתא proves the basic idea that a barrier lets a city measure from its edge. On its own it does not prove the four-אמות height. That detail rests on רב יוסף's reasoning in step 11.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: מְנָא אָמֵינָא לַהּ?
phrases.english: Rav Yosef said: From where do I say this?
As it was taught (in a baraita):
Rabbi permitted that the people of Geder
may go down to Ḥamtan,
but the people of Ḥamtan may not go up to Geder.
What is the reason?
Is it not because these (Geder) made a barrier,
phrases.notes: So גדר measured from its edge and reached חמתן.

phrases.english: and those (Ḥamtan) did not make a barrier?!
phrases.notes: So חמתן measured from each house and fell short of גדר.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the rule from step 9 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רב הונא's rule that a barrier at a ravine's edge lets the city measure its תחום from that edge
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: רבי allowed people of גדר to go down to חמתן, but not people of חמתן to go up to גדר
steps.whatToRemember: With a barrier, the city measures from its edge (גדר). Without one, each person measures from his house (חמתן). That is why the walking permission went in only one direction.

steps.title: The ruling was about violence, not barriers
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי says the people of גדר used to attack the people of חמתן. So the word 'permitted' in the ברייתא really means 'enacted', a safety rule, not a law about תחומין.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came from ארץ ישראל, he said: The people of גדר used to beat up the people of חמתן. And what does 'permitted' mean? It means 'enacted' (made a protective rule).
steps.whatsHappening: רב דימי pushes away רב יוסף's proof from step 12. He gives a totally different reason for רבי's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יוסף read the ברייתא as a תחומין ruling that depended on גדר having a barrier. רב דימי says it was a social enactment: people from חמתן were kept from going up to גדר so they would not get beaten. If that is the reason, the ברייתא proves nothing about barriers.

keyTerms.meaning: When [he] came (usually from ארץ ישראל to בבל, bringing a teaching)
They would really attack / beat up
He enacted (made a protective rule, a תקנה)

steps.confusionAlert: 'Permitted' here does not mean רבי decided the halacha of the תחום allows it. According to רב דימי, it is a public-safety enactment. That is why the proof from step 12 falls away.
steps.whyThisMatters: Once the ברייתא is explained another way, רב יוסף's rule about a tall barrier no longer has this ברייתא as support.

phrases.english: When Rav Dimi came, he said:
phrases.notes: He came from ארץ ישראל to בבל.

phrases.english: They would really assault them,
phrases.notes: The doubled verb means 'really' or 'regularly' attack.

phrases.english: the people of Geder [attacked] the people of Ḥamtan.
And what does 'permitted' mean? He enacted.
phrases.notes: So 'permitted' in the ברייתא really means he made a protective rule, a תקנה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רב יוסף's reading of the ברייתא in step 12 by giving a different reason for רבי's ruling.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the ברייתא of גדר and חמתן for the tall-barrier rule.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ruling can be explained as a safety enactment against violence, so it need not depend on a barrier at all.

steps.title: Why only on שבת?
steps.stepSummary: If the rule was about fights, why did רבי make it only for שבת?
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is different about שבת?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question about רב דימי's explanation. The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fights could happen any day of the week. So why would a safety rule apply only on שבת? The question accepts רב דימי's reason and only wants the detail explained.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different? (asking why one case differs from another)

phrases.english: And what is different about Shabbat?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for a detail of רב דימי's explanation.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the anti-violence enactment applied specifically on שבת.

steps.title: Drunkenness is common on Shabbat
steps.stepSummary: On שבת people eat and drink a lot, so drunkenness is common and fights are more likely.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because drunkenness is common on it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 14.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Big שבת meals with wine lead to more drinking. Drunk people fight more easily, so the danger was greatest on שבת. That is why the enactment was made for that day.

phrases.english: Because drunkenness is common on it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Drunkenness is common on שבת, so violence is more likely then.

steps.title: Won't they fight in חמתן too?
steps.stepSummary: The rule still lets the people of גדר go down to חמתן. Won't they beat up the people of חמתן there as well?
steps.simpleTranslation: When they [the people of גדר] go there [to חמתן], won't they also attack them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges whether רבי's enactment actually works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule only stops the people of חמתן from going up to גדר. But the attackers are allowed to go down to חמתן. If they are the violent ones, they could start fights there too, so the rule would not prevent violence.

phrases.english: When they go there,
won't they also attack them?

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אָזְלִי לְהָתָם נָמֵי מְטַטְרְגִי לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how effective the enactment from step 13 is.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב דימי's explanation that the rule was enacted to prevent violence.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The attackers are still allowed into the victims' town, so the danger is not removed.

steps.title: A dog away from home doesn't bark
steps.stepSummary: A popular saying: a dog outside its own place does not bark for seven years. The people of גדר are bold only on their home turf.
steps.simpleTranslation: A dog not in its own place will not bark for seven years.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 16 with a well-known saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People act tough at home but feel unsure in someone else's town. The people of גדר would not start fights in חמתן, so letting them go there is safe. Only the trip from חמתן up to גדר is dangerous.

phrases.english: A dog not in its own place
does not bark for seven years.

steps.triggerLanguage: כַּלְבָּא בְּלָא מָתֵיהּ שַׁב שְׁנִין לָא נָבַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explanation from human behavior, using a proverb
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The people of גדר will be just as violent in חמתן.
steps.terutzMaskana: Outside their own town they are timid and will not start fights.

steps.title: Won't חמתן take revenge?
steps.stepSummary: If so, now the people of חמתן, who are on their home turf, should attack the visitors from גדר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now too, the people of חמתן will attack the people of גדר!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns the dog saying around and raises a new challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By the logic of step 17, the home side is the bold one. So when visitors from גדר come down, the people of חמתן would be bold at home and might take revenge. Then the rule would still lead to fights.

phrases.english: Now too, they will attack:
the people of Ḥamtan [will attack] the people of Geder!

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשְׁתָּא נָמֵי מְטַטְרְגִי בְּנֵי חַמָּתָן לִבְנֵי גָדֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the logic of step 17's answer to create a new problem.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer in step 17 that home-turf people are the bold ones.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If being at home makes people bold, then חמתן, at home, would attack the visitors from גדר.

steps.title: גדר won't be pushed around that much
steps.stepSummary: The people of גדר would not let themselves be bullied to that extent. They would fight back, so חמתן would not dare attack them.
steps.simpleTranslation: They are not submissive to them to that extent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 18 and closes this discussion of רב דימי's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Visitors from גדר would not start a fight in חמתן, but they would hit back if attacked. Knowing this, the people of חמתן would not start up with them. So the visit from גדר to חמתן is safe in both directions, and only the trip from חמתן to גדר needed to be stopped.

keyTerms.meaning: To such an extent, that much

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב דימי, רבי's rule for גדר and חמתן was a שבת safety enactment against drunken fights, not a תחומין ruling. That is why the ברייתא cannot prove רב יוסף's rule about a tall barrier.

phrases.english: They do not submit to them to that extent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 18 and completes the defense of רב דימי's explanation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The people of חמתן would attack the visitors from גדר on their home turf.
steps.terutzMaskana: The visitors from גדר would fight back, so חמתן would not dare start a fight. The enactment works.

steps.title: The bow-shaped city explanation
steps.stepSummary: רב ספרא explains the one-way rule with a תחום reason: גדר was shaped like a bow.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ספרא said: גדר was a city shaped like a bow.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ספרא gives a different explanation for why the people of גדר may go to חמתן while the people of חמתן may not come to גדר. His reason is based on how the שבת limit is measured, not on fighting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: גדר curved like a bow, and its two ends were less than 4000 אמה apart. For people living in גדר, we pretend the empty space inside the bow is filled with houses and measure from the imaginary bowstring, so חמתן falls inside their limit. For people coming from חמתן there is no such pretending, so the houses along the curve of גדר are beyond their limit.

keyTerms.meaning: A city shaped like a bow (curved)
A bow, the weapon. The straight line joining its two ends is the 'bowstring'

steps.confusionAlert: The same empty space inside the bow counts as 'filled in' for גדר's own residents but as empty space for outsiders from חמתן. That is exactly why the rule only works in one direction.

phrases.english: Rav Safra said:
It (Geder) was a city shaped like a bow.
phrases.notes: The תחום שבת of its residents is measured from the imaginary bowstring.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different technical תחום reason for the ברייתא of step 12, as an alternative to רב דימי's social explanation (step 13). Like רב דימי's, it explains the one-way rule without a barrier, so it also undercuts רב יוסף's proof.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case: the asymmetry comes from the city's geography and how the תחום is measured.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The one-way rule must come either from גדר having a barrier (רב יוסף) or from a safety enactment against fights (רב דימי).
steps.terutzMaskana: Because גדר is bow-shaped, its residents' limit reaches חמתן, but חמתן's limit does not reach all of גדר.

steps.title: The large city and small city explanation
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי בר חיננא says גדר was a large city and חמתן a small one.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב דימי בר חיננא said: they were the people of a large city (גדר) and the people of a small city (חמתן).
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא gives another technical explanation of the one-way rule. He says it depends on the difference in size between the two cities.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Measured from big גדר, the 2000 אמה run past the far end of small חמתן, so its people may walk all of חמתן. Measured from small חמתן, the 2000 אמה run out partway into big גדר, so its people may not walk through all of גדר. This is the same rule as the large-city/small-city reading discussed at the start of the amud (steps 1–2).

phrases.english: Rav Dimi bar Ḥinana said:
They were residents of a large city (Geder)
and residents of a small city (Ḥamtan).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel technical explanation that sits alongside רב ספרא's.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case: the asymmetry comes from the cities' different sizes.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The one-way rule must come either from גדר having a barrier (רב יוסף) or from a safety enactment against fights (רב דימי).
steps.terutzMaskana: Big גדר's limit covers all of חמתן, but small חמתן's limit covers only part of גדר.

steps.title: A second version of who said which answer
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא taught the names as above, while רב טביומי taught that the two explanations were given without saying who said which.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא taught it this way, as stated above. רב טביומי taught it this way: רב ספרא and רב דימי בר חיננא disagreed. One said it was a bow-shaped city, and the other said they were residents of a small city and a large city.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא records two ways the tradition was passed down. The same two answers appear in both versions. The only difference is whether each answer is tied to a specific name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רב כהנא's version, each explanation is clearly assigned to one אמורא. In רב טביומי's version, we only know that רב ספרא and רב דימי בר חיננא gave these two answers, using 'חד אמר... וחד אמר', but not which one gave which. Nothing changes in the halacha. This is only about how the tradition was reported.

keyTerms.meaning: One said... and one said (the speakers are not identified)

steps.whatToRemember: There are two technical reasons for the גדר/חמתן rule: a bow-shaped city, and a large city versus a small city. Different versions disagree only about who said which.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana taught it this way (as above).
Rav Tavyomi taught it this way:

phrases.aramaic: רַב סָפְרָא וְרַב דִּימִי בַּר חִינָּנָא,
phrases.english: Rav Safra and Rav Dimi bar Ḥinana disagreed,

phrases.aramaic: חַד אָמַר: עִיר הָעֲשׂוּיָה כְּקֶשֶׁת הֲוַאי,
phrases.english: one said: it was a city shaped like a bow,
and one said: they were residents of a small city
and residents of a large city.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב כָּהֲנָא מַתְנֵי הָכִי. רַב טַבְיוֹמֵי מַתְנֵי הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reports a different version of who said steps 20 and 21.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both explanations stand. The versions differ only in whether each one is assigned to a named speaker.

steps.title: New משנה: walking through an entire city
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that people of a large city may walk through an entire small city, and people of a small city may walk through an entire large city.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: Residents of a large city may walk through all of a small city, and residents of a small city may walk through all of a large city.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins with a general rule about walking through an entire city on שבת. The next step will explain how this works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule works in both directions. City size makes no difference: the visitor may cover the whole city, even if part of it is more than 2000 אמה from where he came.

keyTerms.meaning: משנה. The opening of a new משנה

phrases.english: MISHNA: The residents of a large city
may walk through an entire small city,
and the residents of a small city
may walk through an entire large city.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה, after the גמרא's discussion of גדר and חמתן ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A visitor may walk through an entire city, large or small, in both directions.

steps.title: The משנה explains: the עירוב is placed inside the city
steps.stepSummary: The משנה explains that its rule applies to someone who placed his עירוב in the other city. He may walk through all of it and 2000 אמה beyond.
steps.simpleTranslation: How so? Someone who was in a large city and placed his עירוב in a small city, or was in a small city and placed his עירוב in a large city, may walk through the whole city and 2000 אמה outside it.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה asks 'כיצד?' (how so?) and then explains its own rule. The key detail is that the person placed his עירוב inside the other city.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once his עירוב is inside a city, that whole city counts as if it were just four אמות. So he may walk through all of it, and his 2000 אמה are measured from the city's edge. This is why the city's size does not matter.

keyTerms.meaning: How so? The משנה is about to explain its own rule
He placed his עירוב (setting his שבת 'home base' there)
Here, an עירוב תחומין: food placed to set a person's שבת base

steps.confusionAlert: Do not confuse this with רב דימי בר חיננא's explanation (step 21), where the people of חמתן could not walk all of גדר. There, they were walking from home with their normal limit. Here, the person placed his עירוב inside the city, so the whole city becomes his base.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the principle that a whole city counts as four אמות for whoever has his עירוב inside it. That principle drives the coming גמרא.
steps.whatToRemember: If your עירוב is inside a city, the entire city counts as your 'spot'. You may walk all of it plus 2000 אמה beyond.

phrases.english: How so?
One who was in a large city
and placed his eiruv in a small city,

phrases.aramaic: בְּעִיר קְטַנָּה וְנָתַן אֶת עֵירוּבוֹ בְּעִיר גְּדוֹלָה —
phrases.english: or was in a small city and placed his eiruv in a large city,
may walk through all of it,
and two thousand cubits beyond it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the general rule of step 23 by describing the exact case: the עירוב was placed in the city.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whoever places his עירוב in a city may walk through the entire city and 2000 אמה beyond it.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא counts the 2000 אמות from the exact spot of the עירוב
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא disagrees with the previous ruling. Someone whose עירוב is in a city gets only 2000 אמות, measured from the exact spot of his עירוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא says: He has only two thousand cubits from the place of his eiruv.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now gives רבי עקיבא's opposing opinion to the rule we just learned. In his view, a person does not get the whole city for free.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion treats the whole city as if it were the person's spot, so he walks the entire city and 2000 אמות beyond it. רבי עקיבא says you start counting from the exact place of the עירוב. That means the area of the city itself uses up part of the 2000 אמות.

keyTerms.meaning: The exact place where his עירוב was put down
Two thousand cubits, the standard walking limit (תחום) on שבת

steps.confusionAlert: רבי עקיבא is not saying the person loses the city. He is saying the city is not free: the city's area is counted as part of the 2000 אמות.

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says:
He has only
two thousand cubits from the place of his eiruv.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A dissenting opinion to the rule in step 24.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone whose עירוב is inside a city gets only 2000 אמות, measured from the exact spot of the עירוב. The city's area counts toward that limit.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא brings proof from an עירוב placed in a cave
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא argues that the חכמים themselves agree about a cave: an עירוב placed there gives only 2000 אמות from its exact spot. A city should be treated the same way.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא said to them: Don't you agree with me that one who places his eiruv in a cave has only two thousand cubits from the place of his eiruv?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא tries to win the argument by pointing to a case the חכמים already accept. He says a city should be no different from a cave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A cave is an enclosed space, much like a city. If the חכמים agree that the cave does not count as one 'spot', the same logic should apply to a city. So the person should get only 2000 אמות from his עירוב.

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva said to them:
Do you not agree with me
regarding one who places his eiruv in a cave,
that he has only
two thousand cubits from the place of his eiruv?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי עקיבא's opinion from step 25.
steps.raayaObject: רבי עקיבא's rule that the 2000 אמות are measured from the exact place of the עירוב.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The case the חכמים accept: an עירוב placed in a cave.

steps.title: The חכמים answer: the cave rule applies only when nobody lives there
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים limit the cave case. Only an empty cave gives just 2000 אמות from the עירוב. A cave where people live counts like a city: you walk all of it and 2000 אמות beyond it.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: When does this apply? When it has no residents. But if it has residents, one may walk through all of it and two thousand cubits beyond it.
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים reject רבי עקיבא's proof. They agree with him only about an empty cave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key factor is whether people live in the place. A lived-in cave is treated like a city, so the whole cave counts as one spot. That means the cave case actually supports the חכמים' rule about cities, not רבי עקיבא's.

keyTerms.meaning: When? (introduces a limit on a rule)
He walks through all of it

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that what makes a place count as one 'spot' is that people live there, not just that it is enclosed.

phrases.english: They said to him: When does this apply?
When it has no residents.
But if it has residents,
one may walk through all of it
and two thousand cubits beyond it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבי עקיבא's proof in step 26.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Partial: the חכמים accept the cave rule only for an empty cave.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רבי עקיבא's proof assumed all caves are treated the same. A lived-in cave is actually treated like a city.

steps.title: The surprising result: inside the cave can be more lenient than on top of it
steps.stepSummary: The rule leads to a surprising outcome. An עירוב inside a lived-in cave gives more walking room than an עירוב on top of the cave.
steps.simpleTranslation: It turns out that its inside is more lenient than its top.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה points out what follows from the חכמים' rule. Being inside the cave can actually give a person more room to walk.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Inside a lived-in cave, you get the whole cave plus 2000 אמות. On top of the cave nobody lives, so you get only 2000 אמות from the spot of the עירוב. So the inner space wins, even though you might have expected the reverse.

keyTerms.meaning: Its top, the area above it

phrases.english: Consequently, its inside is more lenient than its top.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws out what follows from the חכמים' answer in step 27.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Under the חכמים, an עירוב inside a lived-in cave gives more walking room than one placed on top of the cave.

steps.title: Someone whose measured 2000 cubits end inside a cave
steps.stepSummary: Someone measuring his 2000 אמות from outside gets exactly 2000, even if the measurement ends partway into a cave. He does not get the rest of the cave.
steps.simpleTranslation: And regarding one who measures, about whom they said 'we give him two thousand cubits': this applies even if the end of his measurement finishes inside a cave.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds a new rule. It covers someone whose עירוב is outside, whose measured limit runs into a cave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'walk the whole place' rule applies only when the עירוב is inside the city or cave. If your 2000 אמות are measured from elsewhere and simply end inside a cave, you stop exactly there. This is true even if people live in the cave.

keyTerms.meaning: One who measures his walking limit

steps.whatToRemember: A city or a lived-in cave counts as one spot only if your עירוב is inside it. Then you walk all of it plus 2000 אמות. If your measured 2000 אמות merely end inside it, you get only the 2000.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the lived-in cave gives extra room to everyone. The extra room comes only from having the עירוב inside it, not from reaching it at the end of a measurement.

phrases.english: And for one who measures, about whom they said
we give him two thousand cubits:
this applies even if the end of his measurement
finishes inside a cave.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a limit on the lived-in cave leniency from step 27.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Someone whose measured 2000 אמות end inside a cave gets exactly 2000 and may not continue through the rest of the cave.
